subject: research/qual-real
professional: a quantitative methodologist in computational social science who uses LLM-assisted annotation (prediction-powered inference, design-based supervised learning) and would first ask: does the claimed correction beat the baseline it should be compared to, is the 'naive' failure a property of automated coding or of how this particular coder was built, and what is the nearest published method?

evidence.correctness: What it is: 166 lines of stdlib Python (qualreal.py 104, test_qualreal.py 62) plus experiments/run.py (93) and figure.py (33); loads GoEmotions file 1, builds a majority-of-raters 'negative emotion' code, a naive-Bayes coder and a 38-word lexicon coder, and scores naive / human-only / PPI estimators of a prevalence and a short-minus-long gap over 500 hand-coded draws; estimators are imported from research/qual-correction/qualml.py. Ran: downloaded goemotions_1.csv (14.2 MB, HTTP 200 through the proxy) into the cache path, ran python3 research/qual-real/experiments/run.py (4.3 s, not the '~10 s' or '1-2 minutes' the README and docstring give): the regenerated results.txt is byte-identical to the committed one (diff empty), so every table in the README reproduces from the seed. Recomputed independently (my own csv loader and regexes in a scratch script, not the author's functions): (1) 5,313 examples with >=3 raters and no 'very unclear' flag, matching the README. (2) Lexicon coder on the 3,188 test items by hand-built confusion counts: sensitivity 0.3747, specificity 0.9278, accuracy 0.7880, kappa 0.3502, positive rate 0.1487, matching results.txt (0.375 / 0.928 / 0.788 / 0.350 / 0.1487). (3) Ratios quoted in prose: 0.143/0.120 = 1.19 ('19% wider') and 0.127/0.120 = 1.06 ('6% wider'), 0.170/0.028 = 6.1 ('six-fold'), 1-0.065 = 93.5% and 1-0.304 = 70% ('94%' and '70%' missed), short n 1,186 + long n 2,002 = 3,188: all consistent. (4) Whole-file short share 1,979 of 5,313 differs from the test-split 1,186 of 3,188 only by the 60/40 split, as expected. Not independently recomputed: the Monte Carlo coverage numbers (I re-ran them via the author's code only; reproduction is exact but that is the author's own engine). Wald intervals at n=200 with prevalence 0.25 are adequate; coverage 0.944-0.968 is as expected.
evidence.completeness: Claims checked from README and PROJECTS.md milestone 2: dataset load and filtering (works); two stand-in coders (work); naive/human/PPI tables at 100/200/400 items (work, reproduce); SVG figure experiments/gap_estimates.svg (exists); live-page line and homepage card (projects.json entry present; research/_homepage/build.py prints ok for 1,066 projects; check_md_links ok). Not done, and said so: PROJECTS.md milestone 2 reads 'with a model behind ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and a deterministic stub'; the project has neither an LLM coder nor a stub interface, only a dict in run.py; README states 'the point of the milestone ... is not done'. Also not done: 27-emotion extension, the other two raw files. The title question 'does PPI work on real hand-coded text' is answered for two weak non-LLM coders only. No LOG.md, no project.json (card lives in projects.json, valid).
evidence.verification: Ran (cd research/qual-real && python3 -m unittest test_qualreal): 6 tests OK in 0.001 s; qual-correction's 6 tests also OK. Seeded four single-token mutations in qualreal.py, each reverted with git checkout -- research/qual-real/qualreal.py (git status clean afterwards): (1) majority rule int(sum(v)*2 > len(v)) changed to >=: all 6 pass, NOT caught (the test uses 3 raters, so a tie never occurs); (2) NaiveBayes denominator (n[1]+2) changed to (n[1]+1), which breaks smoothing so probabilities can exceed 1: all 6 pass, NOT caught (the NB test only checks two toy words); (3) the guard len(g) >= 5 in estimates() changed to >= 0: all pass, NOT caught (no test with a tiny or empty gold subset); (4) accuracy denominator len(human) changed to len(human)+1: 1 failure, caught. So 1 of 4 caught. Untested: group-level estimates with a restricted `members` set (the gap path that supplies the headline), the NB threshold step in run.py, the CSV loader's text/token path beyond one toy file, and the whole experiment loop. The strong point is that the entire results.txt is seeded and byte-reproducible, which is a regression test in effect, but nothing runs it in CI (research-ci.yml only runs programme_check tests by grep).
evidence.craft: Read qualreal.py, test_qualreal.py, experiments/run.py, the head of figure.py and the estimators in qual-correction/qualml.py. Good: small, typed-by-docstring, stdlib only, seeded, no committed comment text, no usernames read, estimators reused not copied, majority vote and unclear filtering correct. Defects: (a) run.py fetch() calls urlretrieve straight onto the cache path, so an interrupted download leaves a truncated CSV that is then treated as complete (no .part rename, no size or hash check); (b) NB threshold is chosen on the same items the model was fit on (see claims and fitness), a design flaw, not a bug; (c) estimates() silently omits 'human' and 'ppi' when fewer than 5 gold items fall in a group, and run.py then drops the draw from the gap rows, so a coverage row can rest on fewer than 500 draws without saying so (the 'draws' column does show it; none here fall short); (d) docstring says '1-2 minutes', README '~10 s', actual 4 s; (e) sys.path.insert import of a sibling project; (f) 3 duplicate texts in the corpus were not de-duplicated (negligible). No dead code.
evidence.claims: Checked: '3,188 comments, human labels, 25.3% negative' backed by results.txt line 3. 'naive reports 13.3% (coverage 0 of 500)' backed (E2 rows). 'gap -0.170 versus -0.028, six-fold' backed. 'PPI coverage 0.94-0.97' backed (0.944-0.968). 'interval wider than human-only, 0.143 vs 0.120' backed. 'coders are not LLMs', 'not done', 'one corpus, one binary code, majority as truth', 'coder trained on same corpus' all stated, which is candid. Data licence and 'no comment text committed, usernames never read' backed (loader reads only id, text and label columns; confirmed). Reference check: Demszky et al. 2020 ACL author list is correct; Angelopoulos et al. Science 382 correct. The weak point is interpretive: the README disclosed that the NB threshold matches the training share but not how much of the headline 13.3% vs 25.3% undercount that creates (see fitness). 'Findings 1: both coders undercount by 10-12 points' is true of these coders, and is presented as a property of naive counting generally. Disclaimer: 'Produced with AI assistance (Claude)' present.
evidence.fitness: Job: a researcher wants to know whether LLM-assisted annotation plus a small hand-coded sample gives valid group comparisons on real text, and to build on a harness. What they get: a reproducible harness on a public corpus where truth is known on every item, which is a good design (they can subsample gold exactly as in the field), and a clean demonstration that differential error, not just overall error, flips a gap by 6x. What they cannot do: swap in an LLM without editing run.py; trust the 13.3% as typical of automated coding. I tested the second: refitting NB on 60% of the training slice and setting the threshold on the held-out remaining 40% (same rule, still no test labels) gives a test positive rate of 0.213 against 0.253 (vs 0.133 as published) and sensitivity 0.334 (vs 0.221), so about two thirds of the published 12-point undercount comes from thresholding on the data the model overfit, not from the task. The differential-error finding (short vs long) is likely robust but I did not re-measure it under that threshold. Nearest prior work, not cited: PPI++ (Angelopoulos, Duchi, Zrnic 2023, power-tuned lambda, which is never wider than classical human-only in the limit and would reverse finding 3); Egami, Hinck, Stewart, Wei (2023) design-based supervised learning for surrogate labels in text, built for exactly this setting; Gligoric et al. (2024) on confidence-driven inference with LLM annotations; Hopkins and King (2010) for proportion estimation from classifier output; Ziems et al. (2024) and Gilardi et al. (2023) on LLMs as annotators. The result 'PPI with lambda=1 is wider than human-only for a weak coder' is therefore a known property that the field already fixed, so as a result it is sound but not new.
evidence.domain: Compared against the PPI paper (Science 2023) and PPI++ (2023): the classical mean estimator with fixed weight 1 on the rectifier is what is implemented. A methodologist would first ask for the power-tuned lambda (a one-line estimator, lambda = cov(f,y)/var(f) type) since it removes the 'PPI is worse than doing nothing' regime, and for a stratified or per-group estimator for the gap (here each group is estimated from the random gold subset falling in it, which is valid but gives random gold sizes per group; a stratified gold draw would be tighter). Matches practice: random gold sample, normal intervals, coverage over 500 draws, known-truth evaluation, human majority treated as gold with the caveat stated. Departures: no accounting for rater noise in the 'truth' (the 3-rater majority is itself ~uncertain; GoEmotions authors report modest inter-rater agreement), no sensitivity of the group definition (cut at 10 words only), 500 draws gives a coverage Monte Carlo s.e. of about 0.01 (so 0.944 vs 0.968 are not distinguishable and the README does not draw conclusions from the difference, which is right).

defects.what: The headline undercount (naive-Bayes 13.3% vs human 25.3%) is largely produced by choosing the decision threshold on the same items the model was fit on, so the positive rate collapses on new data. With the threshold set on a held-out slice of the training data the test positive rate is 21.3% and sensitivity 0.334 (published 0.221). The README discloses the threshold rule but not its effect on the headline.

PPI is only the fixed-weight (lambda=1) estimator, so finding 3 ('PPI is wider than human-only') is an artefact of that choice; PPI++ power tuning and DSL (Egami et al. 2023) are the standard fixes and nearest prior work, and are neither used nor cited.

Tests would not catch three of four seeded bugs: tie-breaking in the majority vote, the naive-Bayes smoothing denominator, and the minimum-gold guard; the group/members path that produces the headline gap is untested, and no CI job runs the project's tests.
fetch() writes the download straight to the cache path, so a truncated download is reused as if complete; no size or hash check.
Run-time claims disagree: run.py docstring '1-2 minutes', README '~10 s', measured 4.3 s.
Milestone 2 as written in PROJECTS.md (LLM behind ANTHROPIC_API_KEY plus deterministic stub) is not implemented; there is no coder interface, only a dict inside run.py.

verdict: A small, honest, fully reproducible harness: the committed results regenerate byte for byte in 4 seconds from a public dataset, the lexicon-coder confusion table, kappa and the prose ratios recompute independently, and the README states clearly that the coders are not LLMs. It does not meet the bar. Verification is weak (one of four seeded mutations caught, headline gap path untested), the central 13.3% vs 25.3% undercount is mostly a thresholding-on-training-data effect (21.3% with a held-out threshold), and the 'PPI does not pay for weak coders' finding rests on the lambda=1 estimator that PPI++ and DSL, the nearest prior work and uncited, already improve on. A researcher could reuse the data pipeline and the known-truth subsampling design; they should not cite the headline numbers as typical of automated coding, and would want an LLM coder and a power-tuned estimator before building on it.
